angle.selected_angle: Post-Soviet Divergence: How Independent States Created Different Turkic Language Futures
angle.rationale: Shifts from essentialist 'Turkic identity' to geopolitical agency: After 1991 Soviet collapse, different states made *policy choices* (Kazakhstan Latin alphabet + Kazakh revitalization; Kyrgyzstan mixed approach; Tatarstan federalism; Uyghur region faced Han-Chinese pressure). Foregrounds institutional decision-making over cultural determinism.

hook.primary_hook: 1991: The Year Turkic Languages Split Into Five Different Futures — One Alphabet at a Time
hook.entry_point: Soviet collapse creates temporal boundary viewers understand. Post-1991: Kazakhstan chose Latin (policy 2023); Kyrgyzstan didn't mandate change; Tatarstan negotiated bilingual federalism; Uyghur region faced Han-Chinese displacement. Four different choices; four different outcomes.
hook.conflict: Not inevitable cultural drift, but institutional *choice* documented through primary sources (government policy documents, parliamentary decisions).

research_foundation.readiness_rationale: Completeness 0.65 reflects MODERATE COMPLETENESS with SIGNIFICANT GEOPOLITICAL BIAS. 9 well-supported claims documented via PRIMARY SOURCES (Kazakhstan 2023 policy, Putin 2017 declaration, Tatarstan 2017 parliament action). However, Chinese academic perspectives on Uyghur policy not equally accessible; CCP counterarguments censored or inaccessible. D5 notes: 'CCP perspective inaccessible or censored; Chinese academic counterarguments not accessed due to language barriers and publication restrictions.' This bias is documented and managed through narrative transparency.
key_strengths: Post-Soviet language policies well-documented via PRIMARY SOURCES (government policy documents, parliamentary decisions)
Kazakhstan Latinization project thoroughly documented (official policy concept 2023)
Kyrgyzstan and Tatarstan language policies documented via official decisions
Comparative institutional analysis strong (state-by-state policy decision comparison)
major_gaps: CCP perspective inaccessible: Chinese academic counterarguments on Uyghur language policy not accessed due to language barriers and publication restrictions
Longitudinal Uyghur proficiency data: No complete metrics on Uyghur language decline in education/media (blocked access to internal Chinese statistics)
Uyghur diaspora-specific transmission loss: Turkish diaspora data doesn't generalize to Uyghur diaspora experience
Russian scholarly perspectives limited: Russian-language sources on Tatarstan/Kyrgyzstan policies underrepresented (English-language research bias)
Implementation metrics for Kazakhstan/Kyrgyzstan 2024-2026: Data lag on recent progress
readiness_conditions: Condition A: Disclose perspective limitations — 'This research is based primarily on Western-language and Central Asian sources. Chinese-language scholarly perspectives on Uyghur bilingual education policy are not equally accessible to this research. Geopolitical context requires transparency: multiple interpretations of the same policy exist.'

Condition B: Frame Uyghur policy as contested, not settled — 'Uyghur language policy is contested between Chinese development framing and international assimilation framing. This documentary presents documented policy changes; interpretation of their meaning and impact varies by perspective.'

Condition C: Note access barriers explicitly — 'Internal Chinese statistics on Uyghur language proficiency decline are not accessible to this research. Assessments rely on international reporting (RFA, academic sources), which have their own perspective limitations.'

Condition D: Avoid 'genocide' framing unless legally established — 'Evidence of Uyghur language displacement is well-documented; Phase C red-team analysis flags 'genocide' as advocacy framing, not legal consensus. Narration should focus on documented policy changes (education language shifts, Mandarin prioritization) without conflating with contested political terminology.'

content_brief.target_audience: Post-Soviet history interest, language policy scholars, Central Asian studies, Uyghur heritage interest (with geopolitical awareness)
content_brief.narrative_approach: Geopolitical-institutional focus + comparative policy analysis + transparent disclosure of perspective limitations and evidence gaps
content_brief.content_warnings: HIGH geopolitical sensitivity on Uyghur language policy (contested framing; Western perspective bias documented; Chinese counterarguments not equally accessible). Frame as institutional analysis, not political advocacy.

narrative_acts.title: Soviet Collapse & Language Moment (1991 turning point)
narrative_acts.content: Soviet Union dissolves; post-Soviet states inherit Cyrillic-based Turkic languages; now independent, they face choice: maintain Soviet script/policy, or pursue own language policies? Map showing post-1991 borders, institutional independence.

narrative_acts.title: Case Study 1: Kazakhstan Latinization (policy choice + implementation)
narrative_acts.content: Kazakhstan Language Policy Concept (2023 official document): transition to Latin alphabet for Kazakh. Why? Stated rationale: Turkic/international integration. Implementation timeline, educational materials showing transition. Success/challenges of alphabet change (language reform is complex).

narrative_acts.title: Case Study 2-3: Kyrgyzstan & Tatarstan (alternative choices)
narrative_acts.content: Kyrgyzstan maintained mixed Cyrillic-Latin approach; not mandated shift. Tatarstan negotiated Russian-Tatar bilingual federalism with Russian Federation (institutional negotiation). Different institutional contexts, different policy outcomes. Comparative timeline showing divergence.

narrative_acts.title: Case Study 4: Uyghur Region (geopolitical constraint vs. policy choice)
narrative_acts.content: Uyghur language faces displacement by Han-Chinese in education/media/public life. Policy framing varies: Chinese perspective emphasizes bilingual education/development; international perspective emphasizes assimilation pressure. Documented policy changes: education language shift, Mandarin prioritization in schools. Acknowledge contested interpretation; present documented evidence; note perspective limitations transparently.

production_scope.visual_style: Geopolitical-institutional focus + maps + policy documents + comparative tables + archival/contemporary footage
primary_visual_assets: Post-1991 political map (showing newly independent states)
Kazakhstan Language Policy Concept (official document on screen)
Educational materials showing Cyrillic→Latin alphabet transition
Kyrgyzstan and Tatarstan official policy documents
Uyghur language policy context (education directives, bilingual signage if available, documented changes)
Alphabet/script examples (Cyrillic vs. Latin Kazakh, etc.)
Street signage showing language variation across regions (contemporary documentation)
production_scope.interview_potential: Medium-High — Post-Soviet language policy scholars, Central Asian studies experts, language reform practitioners, (Chinese scholarly perspective not equally accessible)

production_notes.historiographic_transparency_required: YES — Perspective limitations must be explicitly stated. Western/Central Asian source dominance documented. CCP perspective accessibility issue flagged.
production_notes.geopolitical_sensitivity: HIGH — Uyghur language policy is politically contested. Framing as institutional analysis, not political advocacy. Multiple interpretations of same policy acknowledged.
caveats_detail: Research perspective bias: 'This research is based primarily on Western-language and Central Asian sources. Chinese-language scholarly perspectives on Uyghur language policy are not equally accessible. Geopolitical context requires transparency: multiple interpretations of the same policy exist.'

Kazakhstan policy complexity: 'Latin alphabet transition is supported by Kazakhstan state but faces practical challenges (implementation timeline, educational transition, cultural attachment to Cyrillic). Policy statement ≠ easy implementation.'

Kyrgyzstan policy rationale: 'Why Kyrgyzstan maintained mixed Cyrillic-Latin approach remains debated. Institutional capacity, cultural preference, and Russian geopolitical influence all likely play roles; precise causality undocumented.'
Tatarstan negotiation dynamics: 'Tatarstan's bilingual federalism reflects negotiation with Russian Federation; precise leverage points and political dynamics incompletely documented.'

Uyghur policy interpretation gap: 'Uyghur language policy is contested between Chinese development framing and international assimilation framing. This documentary presents documented policy changes (education language shifts, Mandarin prioritization); interpretation of their meaning and impact varies by perspective. Avoid contested political terminology ('genocide'); focus on documented institutional changes.'

Access barriers to Chinese data: 'Internal Chinese statistics on Uyghur language proficiency decline are not accessible to this research. Assessments rely on international reporting (RFA, academic sources), which have their own perspective limitations.'
Uyghur diaspora data gap: 'Specific Uyghur diaspora language-transmission loss rates differ from Turkish diaspora patterns and remain incompletely documented.'
